# Tidal Locking and Its Profound Influence on Planetary Climates

Tidal locking occurs when a planet's rotation period matches its orbital period, causing one hemisphere to face its star permanently. This phenomenon, common among planets orbiting red dwarf stars, creates some of the most extreme and fascinating climates in the universe.

The most obvious consequence is the dramatic temperature contrast between hemispheres. The dayside, under perpetual stellar bombardment, can reach temperatures of hundreds of degrees, while the nightside plunges to frigid extremes where atmospheres may even freeze out. On a tidally locked exoplanet, the substellar point becomes a region of permanent noon, while the antisolar point endures eternal night.

However, this doesn't necessarily doom such worlds to being uninhabitable. Atmospheric and oceanic circulation can redistribute heat remarkably effectively. Climate models suggest that planets with thick atmospheres or deep oceans can maintain moderate temperatures across much of their surface. Winds on tidally locked planets often flow from dayside to nightside at the surface, returning aloft, creating a global heat pump that prevents atmospheric collapse.

Water plays a crucial role in these climates. Many models predict an "eyeball Earth" configuration, where a single ocean sits beneath the substellar point, surrounded by ice. Alternatively, a "lobster" pattern may emerge with an ice-free corridor connecting hemispheres. Precipitation patterns concentrate around the dayside, potentially creating permanent storms near the substellar region
